title: ITD 145 Exam 2 Extra Practice
description: 81 more questions on the same topics, for when you want more reps than the main review gives you.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'as' keyword in 'import pandas as pd'?
options: It makes the library run faster
It imports only part of the library
It gives the imported library a shorter alias
questions.explanation: The alias lets you write pd.DataFrame instead of pandas.DataFrame.

questions.question: array1.shape is a method, so you must write array1.shape() with parentheses.
questions.explanation: shape and size are attributes (stored values), written without parentheses.

questions.question: What is the result of multiplying a NumPy array by 2, as in data * 2?
options: The array is repeated twice, end to end
Only the first element is doubled
questions.explanation: NumPy arithmetic is element-wise. With a Python list, data * 2 would repeat the list instead.

questions.question: What is one advantage of an ndarray over a Python list for numeric work?
options: It can hold text and numbers mixed together
It is faster and more memory-efficient and supports whole-array arithmetic
It can grow automatically without limit
It does not need to be imported
questions.explanation: Homogeneous dtype and vectorized operations are the main benefits.

questions.question: What does array1.ndim return for np.array([[1,2],[3,4]])?
questions.explanation: ndim is the number of dimensions (axes). A table of rows and columns has 2.

questions.question: What is the length of np.arange(0,30,6)?
questions.explanation: The values are 0, 6, 12, 18 and 24 - five elements.

questions.question: What does np.zeros((3,4)) create?
questions.explanation: Passing a tuple gives the shape: 3 rows and 4 columns.

questions.question: What is the size of np.zeros((3,4))?
questions.explanation: 3 x 4 = 12 elements.

questions.question: Which call is the correct way to create a 2x3 array of random floats?
questions.explanation: The shape must be passed as a single tuple, hence the double parentheses.

questions.question: In np.arange(2, 20, 4), what does the 4 represent?
options: The number of values to create
questions.explanation: The three arguments are start, stop, step. The result is [2 6 10 14 18].

questions.question: np.array([1, 2, 3]) has how many dimensions?
questions.explanation: A flat list produces a one-dimensional array; its shape is (3,).

questions.question: Why must the import statement come before the code that uses NumPy?
options: The import statement sorts the code that follows
Python does not know what np refers to until the library has been imported
Imports run only at the end of a program
questions.explanation: Using np before import np raises a NameError.

questions.question: What does np.percentile(data, 50) return?
questions.explanation: The 50th percentile is the middle value of the sorted data.

questions.question: np.max(a) returns the largest value in the array.
questions.explanation: max is an aggregate: many values in, one value out.

questions.question: How does np.percentile(a, 25) differ from np.quantile(a, 0.25)?
options: They give the same result; percentile uses a 0-100 scale and quantile uses 0-1
questions.explanation: Same statistic, different scale for the second argument.

questions.question: What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
options: Q3 minus Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of the data
questions.explanation: IQR ignores the extremes, so outliers barely affect it.

questions.question: In the matrix returned by np.corrcoef(x, y), what are the values on the diagonal?
options: The means of x and y
Always 1, because each variable correlates perfectly with itself
questions.explanation: The off-diagonal entries hold the correlation between x and y.

questions.question: Which pandas call returns the correlation between every pair of numeric columns?
questions.explanation: df.corr() returns a matrix of pairwise correlations.

questions.question: If a = np.array([1,2,3]), what is a * 10?
questions.explanation: The single number is broadcast across every element.

questions.question: What does the standard deviation measure?
options: How spread out the values are around the mean
The largest gap between neighbouring values
questions.explanation: A small std means values cluster tightly around the mean.

questions.question: For a 2-D array a, what does a.sum(axis=1) return?
questions.explanation: axis=1 collapses across the columns, leaving one value for each row.

questions.question: What does df.tail(3) return?
questions.explanation: tail(n) returns the last n rows.

questions.question: A Series has both a set of values and an index of labels.
questions.explanation: The index is what lets pandas align data by label.

questions.question: Inside df.query(), you must put column names in quotes.
questions.explanation: Column names appear bare inside the string. Only string values need quotes.

questions.question: What is the main syntactic difference between df[df['x'] > 10] and df.query('x > 10')?
options: The first uses a Python boolean expression; the second uses a string expression
The first is for columns, the second for rows
The first cannot use comparison operators
questions.explanation: Both give the same rows; only the way the condition is written differs.

questions.question: What is the boolean mask df['x'] > 10 on its own?
options: A Series of True/False values, one per row
questions.explanation: The mask is then used inside brackets to keep the True rows.

questions.question: What does df.shape return for a DataFrame with 100 rows and 4 columns?
questions.explanation: shape gives (rows, columns).

questions.question: Which call shows each column's data type and count of non-null values?
questions.explanation: describe() gives summary statistics; info() gives structure.

questions.question: What is the difference between unique() and nunique() on a column?
options: unique() returns the distinct values; nunique() returns how many there are
unique() returns a count; nunique() returns the values
questions.explanation: unique -> the values; nunique -> a number.

questions.question: How would you find how many rows are in a DataFrame?
questions.explanation: df.shape[0] also gives the row count.

questions.question: Which code creates a DataFrame from a dictionary?
questions.explanation: Dictionary keys become column names and the lists become the columns.

questions.question: You want to keep every row but blank out values that fail a condition. Which is best?
questions.explanation: where preserves the shape and replaces failing values with NaN.

questions.question: Which code creates a Series?
questions.explanation: pd.Series takes a list (or array) of values.

questions.question: In df.drop(['a'], axis=1), what does axis=1 mean?
questions.explanation: axis=0 is rows (the default), axis=1 is columns.

questions.question: df.rename(columns={'old':'new'}) changes df in place unless you reassign or use inplace=True.
questions.explanation: It returns a new DataFrame; the original is unchanged unless you reassign or set inplace=True.

questions.question: pd.read_csv() returns a DataFrame.
questions.explanation: Assign it: df = pd.read_csv('file.csv').

questions.question: What does pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=1) do?
options: Places the DataFrames side by side, adding columns
Merges on the index and key
questions.explanation: axis=1 joins along columns; axis=0 (default) joins along rows.

questions.question: What is a potential side effect of concat() on the index?
options: The original index labels are kept, so duplicate labels can appear
questions.explanation: Use ignore_index=True to renumber 0..n-1.

questions.question: Which merge type keeps all rows from both tables, filling gaps with NaN?
questions.explanation: outer = everything from both sides.

questions.question: Which merge type keeps every row of the left table plus matches from the right?
questions.explanation: Left join: the left table is preserved in full.

questions.question: Which statement gives every row of a new column 'flag' the value 1?
questions.explanation: Assigning a single value fills the whole column.

questions.question: What does df.drop(index=[0, 1]) remove?
options: The rows with index labels 0 and 1
questions.explanation: drop by index removes rows; drop by columns removes columns.

questions.question: Why might you choose a pickle over a CSV to save a DataFrame?
options: It can be opened in a text editor
It works in other languages by default
It preserves data types and the index exactly
questions.explanation: CSV must re-infer types on load; pickle stores them.

questions.question: To add the columns of a second table to the first by matching on 'id', which call is appropriate?
questions.explanation: on= names the key column that both tables share.

questions.question: Two DataFrames have the same columns and you want to add the second one's rows to the first. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Same columns and types - append rows with concat.

questions.question: What does df.reset_index(drop=True) do differently?
options: It creates a fresh RangeIndex and discards the old index instead of keeping it as a column
questions.explanation: Useful after filtering when the old labels are not needed.

questions.question: set_index() and reset_index() are inverse operations.
questions.explanation: One moves a column to the index; the other moves it back.

questions.question: After filtering rows with df[df['x'] > 10], the index is:
options: Unchanged - the surviving rows keep their original labels
questions.explanation: The labels can therefore have gaps. reset_index(drop=True) closes them.

questions.question: Why is reset_index() commonly used after groupby()?
options: groupby puts the group keys in the index; reset_index turns them back into ordinary columns
To convert the result to a Series
questions.explanation: Alternatively use as_index=False in groupby.

questions.question: Which statement about a RangeIndex is true?
options: It must be typed in manually
It is generated automatically and counts up from 0
It is created only by set_index
questions.explanation: It is what you get by default.

questions.question: What is a typical reason to use set_index()?
options: To look up rows by a meaningful label such as an ID
questions.explanation: Labels make rows addressable by name rather than position.

questions.question: What is the effect of reset_index() on a multi-index?
options: The index levels become regular columns and a RangeIndex is restored
questions.explanation: It flattens the hierarchy.

questions.question: What does df.dropna(how='all') do?
options: Removes every row with any missing value
Removes only rows in which every value is missing
questions.explanation: how='all' is much more conservative than the default 'any'.

questions.question: Mean-fill computes the average using the missing values as zeros.
questions.explanation: The mean ignores NaN by default.

questions.question: dropna() changes the number of rows, but fillna() does not.
questions.explanation: fillna keeps every row; dropna deletes some.

questions.question: Which call identifies duplicate rows without removing them?
questions.explanation: duplicated() returns a True/False Series marking repeats.

questions.question: How do you drop duplicates judged only on the column 'email'?
questions.explanation: subset restricts the comparison to the named columns.

questions.question: Which method returns True for values that are NOT missing?
questions.explanation: notnull() is the opposite of isnull().

questions.question: How would you drop only rows where 'price' is missing?
questions.explanation: subset limits the check to the named column(s).

questions.question: Which is a reason to impute rather than drop rows with missing data?
options: It is required before any plot
questions.explanation: Dropping can shrink the data set and bias results.

questions.question: A column has values 5, NaN, NaN, 9. After ffill, the column is:
questions.explanation: Each gap copies the last valid value above it.

questions.question: A column has values 5, NaN, NaN, 9. After bfill, the column is:
questions.explanation: Each gap copies the next valid value below it.

questions.question: Why might you fill with the median instead of the mean?
options: The median is less affected by extreme values
The median works only on text
questions.explanation: Outliers pull the mean but hardly move the median.

questions.question: Which statement best compares stack and unstack?
options: They are inverse operations that reshape between long and wide formats
questions.explanation: One lengthens, the other widens.

questions.question: After groupby(), the group keys become the index of the result.
questions.explanation: reset_index() or as_index=False turns them back into columns.

questions.question: stack() makes a DataFrame wider.
questions.explanation: stack makes it longer (narrower). unstack widens.

questions.question: What is the difference between count() and size() in a groupby?
options: size() counts non-null only; count() counts all rows
count() counts non-null values; size() counts all rows including nulls
questions.explanation: The gap appears when a column has missing values.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of steps in groupby?
questions.explanation: Split into groups, apply a function, combine the results.

questions.question: Which call totals sales for each month/product pair in a wide grid?
questions.explanation: pivot() does not take an aggfunc; pivot_table() does.

questions.question: Which call finds the highest salary in each department?
questions.explanation: Group, select the column, aggregate.

questions.question: Long format usually means:
options: Few columns and many rows, with one observation per row
questions.explanation: stack produces long format; unstack/pivot produce wide.

questions.question: What does as_index=False do in groupby?
options: Keeps the group keys as ordinary columns instead of putting them in the index
questions.explanation: It has the same effect as calling reset_index() afterwards.

questions.question: In a boxplot, what does the line inside the box represent?
questions.explanation: The box edges are Q1 and Q3.

questions.question: pandas' df.plot() draws using matplotlib.
questions.explanation: pandas plotting is a convenient wrapper around matplotlib.

questions.question: The box in a boxplot spans from Q1 to Q3.
questions.explanation: The box height is the interquartile range.

questions.question: Which call adds a title to a matplotlib plot?
questions.explanation: Also plt.xlabel() and plt.ylabel() for the axis labels.

questions.question: Which call draws a histogram of one DataFrame column?
questions.explanation: df['col'].plot(kind='hist') is equivalent.

questions.question: Which call draws a boxplot of the numeric columns in a DataFrame?
questions.explanation: df.plot(kind='box') also works.

questions.question: Which plot is the best first check before relying on a correlation coefficient?
questions.explanation: It shows whether the relationship is roughly linear or driven by outliers.

questions.question: How does a histogram differ from a bar chart?
options: A histogram is for text; a bar chart is for numbers
A histogram bins a continuous numeric variable; a bar chart compares distinct categories
questions.explanation: Histogram bars represent numeric ranges.

questions.question: What is the IQR shown by in a boxplot?
questions.explanation: IQR = Q3 - Q1, the middle 50% of the data.
